abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework termed Distributed Cognition for Interactive Systems (DCIS), which reconceptualizes human-computer interaction through the lens of cognitive systems engineering. Traditional HCI theory has predominantly focused on individual user cognition or simplistic stimulus-response models, failing to adequately address the complex sociotechnical ecosystems characterizing contemporary interactive environments. DCIS posits that cognition emerges from dynamic interactions among users, artifacts, and computational systems operating as integrated cognitive systems. The proposed framework synthesizes concepts from distributed cognition, activity theory, and ecological interface design to provide analytical tools for understanding how cognitive load is distributed across human and technological actors. Through extensive analysis of three diverse interaction paradigms—collaborative editing platforms, ambient display systems, and augmented reality interfaces—we demonstrate the framework's explanatory power and predictive validity. Results indicate that DCIS enables designers to identify previously unrecognized cognitive bottlenecks and design intervention points that optimize system-wide performance. This paradigmatic shift from individualistic to distributed cognitive models represents a fundamental reorientation of HCI theory, offering new directions for research in cognitive ergonomics and user interface design. The framework contributes to the theoretical foundations of human-computer interaction by providing a more ecologically valid account of how users engage with complex interactive systems.

Despite the widespread adoption of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) in human-computer interaction research, existing formulations exhibit significant limitations in addressing the affective dimensions of user experience in contemporary interactive systems. This paper presents an Extended Technology Acceptance Model (ETAM) that substantially advances theoretical understanding by integrating constructs from thepleasure-arousal-dominance model and flow theory into the classical TAM framework. The proposed model addresses the implicit assumption in traditional acceptance models that user decisions are primarily cognitive-rational processes, neglecting emotional and experiential factors that increasingly characterize user engagement with modern interactive technologies. Through structural equation modeling analysis of data collected from 847 participants across six distinct application domains, we empirically validate the extended model's superior explanatory power compared to classical TAM formulations. The results demonstrate that the ETAM explains 31% more variance in behavioral intention than the original model, with affective constructs mediating the relationship between perceived usefulness and user acceptance. The extended framework provides improved predictive validity across diverse interaction contexts, from productivity software to entertainment applications. This theoretical refinement contributes to HCI methodology by offering researchers and practitioners a more comprehensive instrument for understanding and predicting technology adoption, while maintaining the parsimony and practical utility that made the original TAM influential.

We present Synaesthetic Interaction Environment (SIE), a novel paradigm for human-computer interaction that enables users to perceive and manipulate digital information through coordinated multisensory feedback integrating auditory, visual, and tactile modalities in real-time. Unlike conventional graphical user interfaces that rely predominantly on visual channels, SIE implements a fundamentally different interaction metaphor where information is represented as dynamic sensory textures that users can explore through natural perceptual-motor patterns. The system architecture comprises custom-designed haptic rendering algorithms, spatial audio synthesis engines, and adaptive visual rendering components that synchronize to create coherent perceptual experiences. A series of controlled experiments with 64 participants evaluated SIE's effectiveness across multiple task domains, including data exploration, spatial navigation, and information visualization. Results demonstrate that the multisensory paradigm enables users to develop more accurate mental models of complex datasets, with performance improvements of 47% in spatial memory tasks and 38% reduction in cognitive load compared to traditional visual-only interfaces. Notably, the benefits were particularly pronounced for users with visual impairments, suggesting that synaesthetic interfaces may fundamentally transform accessibility in computing. This work establishes a new paradigm for interaction design, demonstrating that moving beyond unimodal visual interfaces toward genuinely multisensory interaction represents a transformative direction for future interactive systems.

This paper presents MetaFlow 2.0, a substantially enhanced adaptive user interface system that significantly advances the state of the art in personalized human-computer interaction. While existing adaptive systems typically respond to user behavior through rigid rule-based mechanisms, MetaFlow 2.0 implements a deep learning architecture that continuously models user cognitive and emotional states to dynamically optimize interface presentation. The system integrates gaze tracking, physiological sensing, and interaction pattern analysis to construct comprehensive user models that capture both explicit preferences and implicit cognitive load indicators. We describe the system's architecture, including its novel attention-weighted adaptation algorithm that prioritizes interface modifications based on predicted cognitive impact. A longitudinal evaluation conducted over 12 weeks with 128 participants in professional productivity contexts demonstrates substantial improvements over predecessor systems and non-adaptive baselines. MetaFlow 2.0 achieved a 52% reduction in task completion time, 41% improvement in user satisfaction scores, and maintained adaptation accuracy above 89% across diverse user populations. The system particularly excelled in reducing cognitive ergonomics issues associated with prolonged computer use, with participants reporting 67% fewer instances of mental fatigue. This work advances HCI methodology by providing empirical evidence that sophisticated user modeling enables interface adaptation that genuinely enhances user experience and usability in real-world deployment contexts.
